       ┌────────────────────┐
       │ GPU VRAM           │
       │                    │
       │ dense/shared       │
       │ model weights      │
       │ KV/state cache     │
       │ HOT EXPERT CACHE   │
       └─────────┬──────────┘
                 │ PCIe
       ┌─────────▼──────────┐
       │ Host RAM           │
       │                    │
       │ COMPLETE EXPERT    │
       │ POOL               │
       └─────────┬──────────┘
                 │
       ┌─────────▼──────────┐
       │ SSD / checkpoint   │
       └────────────────────┘
             SLOW / LARGE

Non-expert weights normally remain GPU resident, while host RAM is the authoritative copy of the routed experts. Everything left in VRAM becomes an elastic expert cache shared across layers. A cache entry represents a complete (layer, expert) rather than independent tensor fragments.

That separation is the fundamental trick.

The FreeToken techniques
Technique	What it accomplishes	Tiny-model analogue
Sparse MoE routing	Only k << E experts execute	32–64 experts, top-1/top-2
Host-resident expert pool	Total model can exceed VRAM	Flash/DRAM holds all experts
Global GPU expert cache	Hot experts execute locally	SRAM/NPU memory expert cache
Routing-aware LRU	Cache follows actual workload	Measure/cache recent experts
Full-layer prefill streaming	Hides bulk weight movement	DMA next expert bank
Double buffering	Transfer N+1 while computing N	Two scratch buffers
CPU/GPU hybrid execution	Misses can execute without transfer	CPU + NPU cooperation
q* scheduling	Chooses transfer vs CPU dynamically	Scheduler based on measured bandwidth
Quantized experts	Reduces RAM and transfer traffic	INT8/INT4 experts
CUDA-graph-compatible routing	Removes host dispatch overhead	Static compiled dispatch graph
CPU SIMD + dequantization	Makes CPU miss path bandwidth-efficient	SIMD fallback kernels
Elastic VRAM allocation	Trades expert cache against KV memory	Dynamic SRAM allocation
FTW expert-bank layout	Avoids runtime repacking	Native packed embedded format
Fast bootstrap	Load directly into final representation	mmap/direct DMA packed weights
Semantic prefix/state caching	Avoids recomputation after context edits	Recursive-state snapshots
Radix KV prefix cache	Reuses common prefixes	Optional small prefix cache
Hardware calibration	Measures real RAM/PCIe behavior	Benchmark flash/DRAM/NPU/CPU

The especially important ones for your project are the expert hierarchy, LRU, hybrid miss handling, packed expert format, quantization, and measurement-based scheduling.

2. Prefill and decode are deliberately treated differently

This is one of FreeToken's more interesting decisions.

During generation, MoE routing is sparse. But during a long prompt, thousands of input tokens collectively tend to touch most experts. FreeToken found that trying to fetch individual experts on demand during prefill therefore doesn't buy much.

Instead it allocates two complete expert-layer buffers. While the GPU executes layer L, it streams the experts for layer L+1. The buffers swap roles.

Conceptually:

time ─────────────────────────────────────────────>

GPU:     compute L0 | compute L1 | compute L2 | compute L3
PCIe:       load L1 |    load L2 |    load L3 | load L4
             ^ overlap ^

buffer A:     L0          L2          L4
buffer B:          L1          L3

On an RTX 5090 the paper reports streaming a 64.4-GB expert pool at roughly 52.7 GB/s during an 8192-token prefill; removing the second buffer reduced throughput materially as prompt size increased.

Your tiny implementation should reproduce this experiment even if the buffers contain only tens or hundreds of KB.

That makes the effect visible rather than merely theoretical.

3. Decode becomes an expert-cache problem

Decode is the opposite.

For one token:

router
   |
   +---- expert 3  ---- cache hit
   +---- expert 17 ---- cache hit
   +---- expert 41 ---- MISS

FreeToken uses temporal locality: adjacent tokens frequently select overlapping experts.

So instead of deciding at startup that "experts 0–31 belong on the GPU," it uses an LRU cache whose contents continuously follow actual routing decisions.

That sounds obvious in hindsight, but it is fundamentally different from static offload.

Your demonstration should expose this explicitly:

Token    Selected experts    cache hit/miss
-----    ----------------    --------------
102        3,17                 H,H
103        3,22                 H,M
104       17,22                 H,H
105        3,41                 H,M

Then graph:

cache hit rate
bytes transferred/token
tokens/sec

against cache capacity.

This could become one of the best demonstrations in the project.

4. FreeToken's cleverest mechanism: q*

Suppose a layer needs four experts that aren't in VRAM.

A simplistic system has two choices:

A: transfer all four → GPU
B: execute all four → CPU

FreeToken instead does both simultaneously.

It measures:

B_P: pinned host→GPU transfer bandwidth
B_H: host-memory expert processing bandwidth

and approximately chooses

$$ q^* = m {B_P \over B_H} $$

where m is the number of missing experts.

So:

               4 missing experts
                      |
          ┌───────────┴──────────┐
          │                      │
    transfer/cache           CPU execute
       expert 41             expert 52
                             expert 59
                             expert 63
          │                      │
        GPU                    CPU
          └───────────┬──────────┘
                      │
                  sum output

Both outputs are exact partial MoE outputs; this is not an approximation of the model.

That distinction is important.

The scheduler is approximating the best resource allocation, not the neural computation.

FreeToken now provides ft bench bw specifically to measure these characteristics on the target machine rather than guessing them from specifications.

For your system I'd generalize this to:

$$ q^* = f(B_\text{flash},B_\text{RAM},B_\text{DMA}, B_\text{CPU},B_\text{NPU}) $$

That might actually become a genuinely interesting embedded-systems research result.

5. FreeToken also removes the scheduler from the critical path

There is a less glamorous but important implementation trick.

FreeToken keeps routing/cache decisions compatible with CUDA graph execution. Routing-dependent work—deduplicating experts, determining hits/misses, choosing LRU victims and translating logical expert numbers into physical slots—runs inside fixed graph machinery rather than bouncing repeatedly through Python/host scheduling.

Its CPU side likewise uses persistent native worker threads pinned to physical cores, SIMD kernels, and in-kernel dequantization.

For a 0.5-TOPS NPU, this lesson may matter even more than on CUDA:

Do not make tiny expert dispatches expensive.

A 30-µs neural expert isn't useful if selecting and launching it costs 100 µs.

That argues strongly for a restricted routing scheme that can be ahead-of-time compiled.

6. Quantization helps twice

FreeToken currently supports combinations including BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and MXFP4 depending on model/backend.

For an offloaded MoE model quantization gives two benefits:

$$ \text{smaller weights} \Rightarrow \begin{cases} \text{more experts fit in cache}\\ \text{less data crosses PCIe} \end{cases} $$

That second property is particularly important.

For your embedded system, INT4 expert weights may therefore be more useful than INT4 dense weights.

The shared network can initially remain INT8 while experts become INT4.

7. FTW is also worth copying conceptually

FreeToken normalizes architecture-specific experts into expert banks keyed by something equivalent to:

expert_id = layer * experts_per_layer + expert

and FTW stores the checkpoint already arranged that way. Loading can therefore read aligned blocks directly into their runtime host representation rather than loading a generic checkpoint and rearranging hundreds of GB afterward.

It also populates host memory before pinning it, avoiding needless zero/fault work on enormous pinned allocations.

Your format might deliberately be extremely simple:

TinyMoE file
├── header
├── tokenizer
├── shared weights
├── routers
├── engram
├── expert-index
├── expert-0000
├── expert-0001
├── ...
└── expert-N

Each expert should be independently DMA-able.

That would make experiments with HDD/SSD/SPI-flash/RAM/external SRAM unusually straightforward.

8. The currently interesting FreeToken models

FreeToken's current known-good model list has moved beyond its original three headline models. The documentation now lists DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.2, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Qwen3.6/3.5 MoE, Qwen3-MoE, GPT-OSS, Gemma-4, MiniMax-M2.5 and Muse-Glimmer variants.

The headline results from the paper remain particularly informative:

Model	Why interesting
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B	Small active footprint; FreeToken reports 77–83 tok/s on RTX 5090
DeepSeek-V4-Flash	284B total, ~13B active; 22–25 tok/s on RTX 5090
GLM-5.2	753B total; demonstrated on a single workstation GPU
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next	Newer architecture, particularly interesting for your memory idea

Those headline performance results come from the FreeToken evaluation.

And there is a rather striking connection to your Engram idea: FreeToken's current model documentation says Qwen3.8-Flash-Next uses a 47.7-GiB PLE n-gram table pinned in host RAM.

That is almost a giant-scale version of one component we're proposing to miniaturize.

9. Now combine this with HRM/TRM

There is an important distinction first:

HRM and TRM are not tiny general-purpose LLMs.

HRM's original model was 27M parameters and obtained striking results on structured reasoning tasks using recurrence and two interacting modules operating at different timescales rather than a deep stack of unique layers.

TRM simplifies the concept dramatically: essentially a tiny recurrent network repeatedly updates a latent state and candidate answer. The original TRM work uses about 7M parameters and only two neural layers.

Some follow-up results also suggest caution about interpreting the headline ARC numbers: performance depends substantially on task conditioning, augmentation, sampling/voting and test-time compute.

But that doesn't weaken the architectural lesson relevant here:

Reasoning depth does not necessarily require parameter depth.

That is exactly what we want.

10. I would build a Recursive Tiny MoE

Rather than:

Transformer layer 0
Transformer layer 1
Transformer layer 2
...
Transformer layer 24

I'd build:

             ┌───────────────────────┐
tokens ─────►│ embedding + Engram    │
             └──────────┬────────────┘
                        ▼
              ┌───────────────────┐
              │ shared recurrent  │◄──────────────┐
              │ reasoning block   │               │
              └───────┬───────────┘               │
                      │                           │
                  router                          │
                 /  |  \                          │
                /   |   \                         │
            expert expert expert                  │
                \   |   /                         │
                 combine                          │
                      │                           │
                update state ─────────────────────┘
                      │
                after R cycles
                      ▼
                    LM head

Unique parameter count stays tiny.

Effective computational depth becomes adjustable.

11. A concrete first architecture

I'd start approximately here:

Component	V0
Vocabulary	4,096
d_model	256
Physical recurrent blocks	4
Recurrences	1–8 selectable
Experts/block	32
Active experts	top-2
Expert hidden width	128
Attention	GQA or very small causal attention
Engram	hashed 2/3/4-gram
Engram slots	65,536
Engram value width	32
Training precision	BF16/FP16
Deployment shared weights	INT8
Deployment experts	INT8 → INT4
Engram	INT8

A gated expert roughly needs:

$$ 3\times256\times128 \approx 98K $$

parameters.

Therefore:

$$ 98K\times32\times4 \approx 12.6M $$

expert parameters total.

Add embeddings, attention, routers and projections and you're probably still around 15–20M parameters.

At INT4:

20M parameters × 0.5 byte ≈ 10 MB

before scales and metadata.

That is almost comically small relative to 256 MB.

So we can afford to increase the experiment substantially later.

12. And this is where "many experts" becomes interesting

Suppose instead we have:

4 blocks
64 experts/block
top-2

We have:

256 experts physically present
  8 expert executions per recurrent sweep

So only:

$$ 8/256 = 3.1\% $$

of the expert population is active during one pass.

If we perform four recurrent iterations:

iteration 0 → experts {7,19,...}
iteration 1 → experts {7,22,...}
iteration 2 → experts {4,22,...}
iteration 3 → experts {4,31,...}

we get something especially interesting:

expert routing over reasoning time

not merely routing over transformer depth.

That could show genuine emergent specialization.

For example:

expert 7   → syntax
expert 12  → arithmetic
expert 22  → identifier relationships
expert 31  → answer refinement

We should not force those meanings.

We should instrument the model and discover whether such specialization develops.

13. Add the Engram as another sparse axis

DeepSeek describes Engram as complementary to MoE:

MoE = conditional computation
Engram = conditional memory

Engram performs deterministic N-gram addressing and retrieves learned memory values in essentially O(1), avoiding the need for neural layers to repeatedly reconstruct common token patterns. DeepSeek also emphasizes that deterministic addressing makes very large tables naturally offloadable.

Our tiny version could be delightfully simple.

For recent tokens:

"for" "(" "i"

compute:

h2 = hash("(" ,"i")       % table_size
h3 = hash("for","(","i")  % table_size

lookup:

E2[h2]
E3[h3]

then:

engram = projection(E2 + E3)

and combine:

$$ h'_t = h_t + g_t\cdot E_\text{ngram} $$

where g is a learned gate.

Initially:

65536 entries
× 32 dimensions
× INT8
≈ 2 MB

Beautifully manageable.

14. There is a useful negative result to keep in mind

A recent independent experiment applying Engram-like tables to small 0.5B–4B models found substantial perplexity improvements but essentially no consistent gain on HellaSwag, PIQA or ARC-Challenge.

That makes your experiment more interesting, not less.

We can directly measure:

                         Perplexity    reasoning    memory      speed
Dense baseline
+ recurrence
+ MoE
+ Engram
+ recurrence + MoE
+ MoE + Engram
+ all three

Instead of assuming that Engram must help.

15. The experimental progression I would use

This is where I think your project can become much more valuable than simply "another tiny LLM."

Stage	Architecture	Question
0	dense tiny transformer	Baseline
1	recurrent shared layers	Does repeated compute replace parameters?
2	dense + Engram	Does external memory improve PPL/tasks?
3	top-1 MoE	Can experts specialize?
4	top-2 MoE	Is quality worth doubled active compute?
5	recurrent MoE	Does expert selection change during reasoning?
6	recurrent MoE + Engram	Do memory and compute sparsity complement each other?
7	quantized	What quality is lost at INT8/INT4?
8	constrained expert cache	What does cache size do?
9	CPU/NPU hybrid	Can FreeToken-style scheduling help?
10	256-MB target	Can the complete architecture survive embedded deployment?

Every stage produces a measurable result.

That is considerably better pedagogically than starting with the final architecture.

16. Distillation: "from scratch" still makes sense

I would interpret "distilled from scratch" as:

Initialize the tiny model randomly, but train it partly from targets produced by a capable teacher.

We're not pruning or compressing an existing network.

We create our own:

tokenizer
architecture
router
experts
Engram
recursive computation

from scratch.

Then a larger teacher generates:

input → teacher output

and, where practical:

teacher token probability distribution

Student objective:

$$ L = \alpha L_\text{token} +\beta L_\text{KD} +\gamma L_\text{router} +\delta L_\text{balance} $$

Potentially later:

$$ +\epsilon L_\text{recurrence} $$

where intermediate recursive states are rewarded for progressively improving the answer.

We don't need a frontier teacher. A modest local 1B–7B model can generate vastly better training labels than our ~20M student.

17. Start with a constrained domain

I would not initially train it to be a general chatbot.

That confounds too many things.

I'd use a mixture like:

natural language
simple code
arithmetic
sequence transformations
logic puzzles
small algorithms
structured text

with synthetic data heavily represented.

Why?

Because then we can actually see whether experts specialize.

Imagine a router eventually producing:

arithmetic → experts 3,17
Rust syntax → experts 8,26
English prose → experts 2,14
sequence reasoning → experts 21,31

That's an educational result you can inspect.

18. Metrics should go far beyond perplexity

For every run I'd record:

Neural	Systems
validation loss	tokens/sec
perplexity	bytes/token
task accuracy	RAM peak
teacher/student KL	accelerator RAM
active params/token	expert cache hit rate
router entropy	expert transfers/token
expert load balance	CPU vs NPU work
expert specialization	energy/token
accuracy vs recursion	latency/token
Engram contribution	Engram collisions
Engram gate magnitude	cache reuse distance

FreeToken demonstrates why this matters: systems characteristics can dominate performance even when the mathematical model remains identical.

19. Your 256-MB / 0.5-TOPS target is plausible — with qualifications

Inference: absolutely plausible for this tiny architecture.

Training the complete system on-device: much less attractive.

A 20M-parameter model may require only about:

INT8   ~20 MB
INT4   ~10 MB

for deployed weights.

But Adam-style training might require roughly:

weights
gradients
master weights
first moment
second moment
activations

and quickly exceed 256 MB.

So I'd separate:

training machine
    ↓
quantized packed checkpoint
    ↓
256-MB inference device

and then optionally support limited on-device learning:

router adaptation
Engram updates
small expert fine-tuning
last-layer training

That would itself be an interesting experiment.

20. 0.5 TOPS probably isn't the real limit

For this design the limiting resource may be:

memory bandwidth and dispatch latency, not TOPS.

Suppose a token touches only ~1–3M parameters through recurrent sparse execution.

Even at several recurrent steps that's nowhere near a 0.5-TOPS theoretical arithmetic ceiling.

But if each tiny expert causes:

flash read
DMA setup
NPU submission
synchronization

the accelerator may spend more time launching experts than multiplying matrices.

Therefore I would design the NPU architecture around expert bundles rather than arbitrary individual networks.

For example:

expert-bank-0 = experts 0..7
expert-bank-1 = experts 8..15
...

and make the router's scheduling granular enough to suit the actual NPU compiler.

21. A more radical option: experts as low-rank deltas

For the smallest machine, I'd also test:

            shared FFN
                +
       selected expert delta

rather than completely separate FFNs.

Each expert becomes:

$$ \Delta W_e = A_eB_e $$

with rank perhaps 4 or 8.

Then you can afford hundreds of experts.

Example:

d = 256
rank = 8

expert parameters
≈ 2 × 256 × 8
= 4096

So:

256 experts ≈ 1M parameters

per expert location.

That gives you genuinely large expert populations while remaining tiny.

This may actually be a better fit for the 0.5-TOPS NPU because the big shared matrix remains static and accelerator-friendly.

22. My preferred eventual architecture

I would call the conceptual design something like µMoE-RM for now:

                   token IDs
                      │
            ┌─────────▼────────┐
            │ token embedding  │
            └─────────┬────────┘
                      │
       recent tokens ─┼─────────────┐
                      │             │
                      │       ┌─────▼─────┐
                      │       │  Engram   │
                      │       │ 2/3/4gram │
                      │       └─────┬─────┘
                      │             │
                 ┌────▼─────────────▼──┐
                 │ recurrent core      │◄──────┐
                 │ attention/state     │       │
                 └────────┬────────────┘       │
                          │                    │
                    ┌─────▼─────┐              │
                    │  router   │              │
                    └─────┬─────┘              │
                          │ top-k               │
                    ┌─────▼─────┐              │
             RAM/   │ expert    │              │
             flash──┤ cache     │              │
                    └─────┬─────┘              │
                          │                    │
             ┌────────────┼────────────┐       │
             │            │            │       │
          expert       expert       expert     │
             │            │            │       │
             └────────────┼────────────┘       │
                          │                    │
                     combine                   │
                          │                    │
                     state update ─────────────┘
                          │
                      LM head

It has three independent kinds of sparsity:

$$ \boxed{ \text{parameter sharing} + \text{conditional compute} + \text{conditional memory} } $$

namely:

recurrence → temporal parameter reuse

MoE       → compute sparsity

Engram    → memory lookup sparsity

FreeToken then adds a fourth:

expert cache → residency sparsity

That is a remarkably elegant little research system.

23. It also fits your older hardware progression unusually well

I would actually develop it downward:

RTX 3090 / 5060
       │
       ▼
normal training + profiling
       │
       ▼
RTX 3060 / P40
       │
       ▼
CPU-only old Xeon
       │
       ▼
small SBC
       │
       ▼
LicheeRV/SG2002-class
256 MB + ~0.5 TOPS NPU

At every step, constrain the previous system artificially:

64 MB expert cache
32 MB
16 MB
8 MB
...

before moving to the real hardware.

Then an embedded failure isn't mysterious—you already know approximately where the knee in the curve should occur.

The experiment I would build first

I would resist starting with language generation.

Build a ~5–10M parameter recurrent MoE, perhaps 16 experts with top-2, and train it on synthetic transformations plus tiny text.

Give it a 64K × 32 ≈ 2-MB Engram.

Then build a visual/instrumented runtime showing:

current token
↓
Engram addresses + retrieved values
↓
recursive iteration 1
    router → experts 3,7
recursive iteration 2
    router → experts 3,12
recursive iteration 3
    router → experts 9,12
↓
prediction

alongside:

expert cache
┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
│ E3 │ E7 │E12 │ E9 │... │
└────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘

hits     7
misses   2
loads    1
CPU      1
NPU      8

Once that works, scale the number of experts upward while keeping active parameters nearly constant.

That gives you a very clean experimental question:

$$ \textbf{How much model capacity can we add without adding proportional compute?} $$

Then add the second question:

$$ \textbf{How much of that capacity actually needs to reside near the accelerator?} $$

And finally the Engram question:

$$ \textbf{How much memorization can be removed from neural computation altogether?} $$

Those three questions connect TRM/HRM → MoE → Engram → FreeToken → your 256-MB NPU target much more coherently than simply trying to shrink an existing LLM.

I think this is strong enough to justify its own experimental repo rather than being merely another sw-mlpl demonstration: the repo could progressively implement Dense → Recursive → MoE → Engram → Cached MoE → Hybrid CPU/NPU, with every stage retaining comparable benchmarks and trace visualizations.

what would we call this new repo?

Given the repo's purpose—a small, inspectable experimental model that combines recursive reasoning, sparse MoE, Engram memory, and FreeToken-inspired memory hierarchy—I'd avoid naming it after any one of those techniques. The interesting thing is the combination.

My strongest candidates:

Name	Why it works
tiny-moe-lab	Immediately understandable; emphasizes experimentation
micro-moe	Short, memorable, emphasizes extreme scaling-down
recursive-moe	Captures perhaps the most novel architectural combination
sparse-reasoner	Describes the goal rather than implementation
tiny-sparse-reasoner	More explicit about scale
micro-reasoner	Nice if MoE/Engram are implementation details
tiny-conditional-model	Captures conditional compute + memory
micro-moe-reasoner	Descriptive without being too long
tiny-moe-research	Serious/academic sounding, but generic
moe-microscope	Excellent if education/visualization is central
I particularly like moe-microscope

It fits what we're actually proposing better than tiny-moe-lab.

The project isn't merely trying to create the smallest useful MoE. It's intended to let someone look inside one:

token
  ↓
Engram lookup ─────────► inspect
  ↓
recurrent state ───────► inspect
  ↓
router ────────────────► inspect
  ↓
expert selection ──────► inspect
  ↓
expert cache ──────────► inspect
  ↓
CPU/NPU scheduling ────► inspect
  ↓
prediction

And experiments can progressively turn mechanisms on:

dense
  → recursive
  → MoE
  → recursive MoE
  → + Engram
  → + quantization
  → + expert caching
  → + heterogeneous execution
  → tiny hardware

That makes moe-microscope a good description of the project's educational purpose rather than just its architecture.

It also connects nicely with the "ML microscope" concept we've discussed for your visualization work without tying the repository to sw-MLPL itself.

Another direction: mi

I think that combination is unusually well suited to an educational/research system because you can make total parameters, active parameters, active experts, memory traffic, recursion depth, Engram size, and cache size independently adjustable.

1. What FreeToken is really doing

FreeToken's starting observation is straightforward: MoE solves the compute problem but does not automatically solve the storage problem. DeepSeek-V4-Flash, for example, routes each token through only 6 of 256 routed experts in each of 43 layers; roughly 13B of its 284B parameters participate in a token even though the complete expert pool is vastly larger.

So FreeToken does not treat VRAM as "where the model lives."

It treats the machine approximately as:

             FAST / SMALL
       ┌────────────────────┐
       │ GPU VRAM           │
       │                    │
       │ dense/shared       │
       │ model weights      │
       │ KV/state cache     │
       │ HOT EXPERT CACHE   │
       └─────────┬──────────┘
                 │ PCIe
       ┌─────────▼──────────┐
       │ Host RAM           │
       │                    │
       │ COMPLETE EXPERT    │
       │ POOL               │
       └─────────┬──────────┘
                 │
       ┌─────────▼──────────┐
       │ SSD / checkpoint   │
       └────────────────────┘
             SLOW / LARGE

Non-expert weights normally remain GPU resident, while host RAM is the authoritative copy of the routed experts. Everything left in VRAM becomes an elastic expert cache shared across layers. A cache entry represents a complete (layer, expert) rather than independent tensor fragments.

That separation is the fundamental trick.

The FreeToken techniques
Technique	What it accomplishes	Tiny-model analogue
Sparse MoE routing	Only k << E experts execute	32–64 experts, top-1/top-2
Host-resident expert pool	Total model can exceed VRAM	Flash/DRAM holds all experts
Global GPU expert cache	Hot experts execute locally	SRAM/NPU memory expert cache
Routing-aware LRU	Cache follows actual workload	Measure/cache recent experts
Full-layer prefill streaming	Hides bulk weight movement	DMA next expert bank
Double buffering	Transfer N+1 while computing N	Two scratch buffers
CPU/GPU hybrid execution	Misses can execute without transfer	CPU + NPU cooperation
q* scheduling	Chooses transfer vs CPU dynamically	Scheduler based on measured bandwidth
Quantized experts	Reduces RAM and transfer traffic	INT8/INT4 experts
CUDA-graph-compatible routing	Removes host dispatch overhead	Static compiled dispatch graph
CPU SIMD + dequantization	Makes CPU miss path bandwidth-efficient	SIMD fallback kernels
Elastic VRAM allocation	Trades expert cache against KV memory	Dynamic SRAM allocation
FTW expert-bank layout	Avoids runtime repacking	Native packed embedded format
Fast bootstrap	Load directly into final representation	mmap/direct DMA packed weights
Semantic prefix/state caching	Avoids recomputation after context edits	Recursive-state snapshots
Radix KV prefix cache	Reuses common prefixes	Optional small prefix cache
Hardware calibration	Measures real RAM/PCIe behavior	Benchmark flash/DRAM/NPU/CPU

The especially important ones for your project are the expert hierarchy, LRU, hybrid miss handling, packed expert format, quantization, and measurement-based scheduling.

2. Prefill and decode are deliberately treated differently

This is one of FreeToken's more interesting decisions.

During generation, MoE routing is sparse. But during a long prompt, thousands of input tokens collectively tend to touch most experts. FreeToken found that trying to fetch individual experts on demand during prefill therefore doesn't buy much.

Instead it allocates two complete expert-layer buffers. While the GPU executes layer L, it streams the experts for layer L+1. The buffers swap roles.

Conceptually:

time ─────────────────────────────────────────────>

GPU:     compute L0 | compute L1 | compute L2 | compute L3
PCIe:       load L1 |    load L2 |    load L3 | load L4
             ^ overlap ^

buffer A:     L0          L2          L4
buffer B:          L1          L3

On an RTX 5090 the paper reports streaming a 64.4-GB expert pool at roughly 52.7 GB/s during an 8192-token prefill; removing the second buffer reduced throughput materially as prompt size increased.

Your tiny implementation should reproduce this experiment even if the buffers contain only tens or hundreds of KB.

That makes the effect visible rather than merely theoretical.

3. Decode becomes an expert-cache problem

Decode is the opposite.

For one token:

router
   |
   +---- expert 3  ---- cache hit
   +---- expert 17 ---- cache hit
   +---- expert 41 ---- MISS

FreeToken uses temporal locality: adjacent tokens frequently select overlapping experts.

So instead of deciding at startup that "experts 0–31 belong on the GPU," it uses an LRU cache whose contents continuously follow actual routing decisions.

That sounds obvious in hindsight, but it is fundamentally different from static offload.

Your demonstration should expose this explicitly:

Token    Selected experts    cache hit/miss
-----    ----------------    --------------
102        3,17                 H,H
103        3,22                 H,M
104       17,22                 H,H
105        3,41                 H,M

Then graph:

cache hit rate
bytes transferred/token
tokens/sec

against cache capacity.

This could become one of the best demonstrations in the project.

4. FreeToken's cleverest mechanism: q*

Suppose a layer needs four experts that aren't in VRAM.

A simplistic system has two choices:

A: transfer all four → GPU
B: execute all four → CPU

FreeToken instead does both simultaneously.

It measures:

B_P: pinned host→GPU transfer bandwidth
B_H: host-memory expert processing bandwidth

and approximately chooses

$$ q^* = m {B_P \over B_H} $$

where m is the number of missing experts.

So:

               4 missing experts
                      |
          ┌───────────┴──────────┐
          │                      │
    transfer/cache           CPU execute
       expert 41             expert 52
                             expert 59
                             expert 63
          │                      │
        GPU                    CPU
          └───────────┬──────────┘
                      │
                  sum output

Both outputs are exact partial MoE outputs; this is not an approximation of the model.

That distinction is important.

The scheduler is approximating the best resource allocation, not the neural computation.

FreeToken now provides ft bench bw specifically to measure these characteristics on the target machine rather than guessing them from specifications.

For your system I'd generalize this to:

$$ q^* = f(B_\text{flash},B_\text{RAM},B_\text{DMA}, B_\text{CPU},B_\text{NPU}) $$

That might actually become a genuinely interesting embedded-systems research result.

5. FreeToken also removes the scheduler from the critical path

There is a less glamorous but important implementation trick.

FreeToken keeps routing/cache decisions compatible with CUDA graph execution. Routing-dependent work—deduplicating experts, determining hits/misses, choosing LRU victims and translating logical expert numbers into physical slots—runs inside fixed graph machinery rather than bouncing repeatedly through Python/host scheduling.

Its CPU side likewise uses persistent native worker threads pinned to physical cores, SIMD kernels, and in-kernel dequantization.

For a 0.5-TOPS NPU, this lesson may matter even more than on CUDA:

Do not make tiny expert dispatches expensive.

A 30-µs neural expert isn't useful if selecting and launching it costs 100 µs.

That argues strongly for a restricted routing scheme that can be ahead-of-time compiled.

6. Quantization helps twice

FreeToken currently supports combinations including BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and MXFP4 depending on model/backend.

For an offloaded MoE model quantization gives two benefits:

$$ \text{smaller weights} \Rightarrow \begin{cases} \text{more experts fit in cache}\\ \text{less data crosses PCIe} \end{cases} $$

That second property is particularly important.

For your embedded system, INT4 expert weights may therefore be more useful than INT4 dense weights.

The shared network can initially remain INT8 while experts become INT4.

7. FTW is also worth copying conceptually

FreeToken normalizes architecture-specific experts into expert banks keyed by something equivalent to:

expert_id = layer * experts_per_layer + expert

and FTW stores the checkpoint already arranged that way. Loading can therefore read aligned blocks directly into their runtime host representation rather than loading a generic checkpoint and rearranging hundreds of GB afterward.

It also populates host memory before pinning it, avoiding needless zero/fault work on enormous pinned allocations.

Your format might deliberately be extremely simple:

TinyMoE file
├── header
├── tokenizer
├── shared weights
├── routers
├── engram
├── expert-index
├── expert-0000
├── expert-0001
├── ...
└── expert-N

Each expert should be independently DMA-able.

That would make experiments with HDD/SSD/SPI-flash/RAM/external SRAM unusually straightforward.

8. The currently interesting FreeToken models

FreeToken's current known-good model list has moved beyond its original three headline models. The documentation now lists DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.2, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Qwen3.6/3.5 MoE, Qwen3-MoE, GPT-OSS, Gemma-4, MiniMax-M2.5 and Muse-Glimmer variants.

The headline results from the paper remain particularly informative:

Model	Why interesting
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B	Small active footprint; FreeToken reports 77–83 tok/s on RTX 5090
DeepSeek-V4-Flash	284B total, ~13B active; 22–25 tok/s on RTX 5090
GLM-5.2	753B total; demonstrated on a single workstation GPU
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next	Newer architecture, particularly interesting for your memory idea

Those headline performance results come from the FreeToken evaluation.

And there is a rather striking connection to your Engram idea: FreeToken's current model documentation says Qwen3.8-Flash-Next uses a 47.7-GiB PLE n-gram table pinned in host RAM.

That is almost a giant-scale version of one component we're proposing to miniaturize.

9. Now combine this with HRM/TRM

There is an important distinction first:

HRM and TRM are not tiny general-purpose LLMs.

HRM's original model was 27M parameters and obtained striking results on structured reasoning tasks using recurrence and two interacting modules operating at different timescales rather than a deep stack of unique layers.

TRM simplifies the concept dramatically: essentially a tiny recurrent network repeatedly updates a latent state and candidate answer. The original TRM work uses about 7M parameters and only two neural layers.

Some follow-up results also suggest caution about interpreting the headline ARC numbers: performance depends substantially on task conditioning, augmentation, sampling/voting and test-time compute.

But that doesn't weaken the architectural lesson relevant here:

Reasoning depth does not necessarily require parameter depth.

That is exactly what we want.

10. I would build a Recursive Tiny MoE

Rather than:

Transformer layer 0
Transformer layer 1
Transformer layer 2
...
Transformer layer 24

I'd build:

             ┌───────────────────────┐
tokens ─────►│ embedding + Engram    │
             └──────────┬────────────┘
                        ▼
              ┌───────────────────┐
              │ shared recurrent  │◄──────────────┐
              │ reasoning block   │               │
              └───────┬───────────┘               │
                      │                           │
                  router                          │
                 /  |  \                          │
                /   |   \                         │
            expert expert expert                  │
                \   |   /                         │
                 combine                          │
                      │                           │
                update state ─────────────────────┘
                      │
                after R cycles
                      ▼
                    LM head

Unique parameter count stays tiny.

Effective computational depth becomes adjustable.

11. A concrete first architecture

I'd start approximately here:

Component	V0
Vocabulary	4,096
d_model	256
Physical recurrent blocks	4
Recurrences	1–8 selectable
Experts/block	32
Active experts	top-2
Expert hidden width	128
Attention	GQA or very small causal attention
Engram	hashed 2/3/4-gram
Engram slots	65,536
Engram value width	32
Training precision	BF16/FP16
Deployment shared weights	INT8
Deployment experts	INT8 → INT4
Engram	INT8

A gated expert roughly needs:

$$ 3\times256\times128 \approx 98K $$

parameters.

Therefore:

$$ 98K\times32\times4 \approx 12.6M $$

expert parameters total.

Add embeddings, attention, routers and projections and you're probably still around 15–20M parameters.

At INT4:

20M parameters × 0.5 byte ≈ 10 MB

before scales and metadata.

That is almost comically small relative to 256 MB.

So we can afford to increase the experiment substantially later.

12. And this is where "many experts" becomes interesting

Suppose instead we have:

4 blocks
64 experts/block
top-2

We have:

256 experts physically present
  8 expert executions per recurrent sweep

So only:

$$ 8/256 = 3.1\% $$

of the expert population is active during one pass.

If we perform four recurrent iterations:

iteration 0 → experts {7,19,...}
iteration 1 → experts {7,22,...}
iteration 2 → experts {4,22,...}
iteration 3 → experts {4,31,...}

we get something especially interesting:

expert routing over reasoning time

not merely routing over transformer depth.

That could show genuine emergent specialization.

For example:

expert 7   → syntax
expert 12  → arithmetic
expert 22  → identifier relationships
expert 31  → answer refinement

We should not force those meanings.

We should instrument the model and discover whether such specialization develops.

13. Add the Engram as another sparse axis

DeepSeek describes Engram as complementary to MoE:

MoE = conditional computation
Engram = conditional memory

Engram performs deterministic N-gram addressing and retrieves learned memory values in essentially O(1), avoiding the need for neural layers to repeatedly reconstruct common token patterns. DeepSeek also emphasizes that deterministic addressing makes very large tables naturally offloadable.

Our tiny version could be delightfully simple.

For recent tokens:

"for" "(" "i"

compute:

h2 = hash("(" ,"i")       % table_size
h3 = hash("for","(","i")  % table_size

lookup:

E2[h2]
E3[h3]

then:

engram = projection(E2 + E3)

and combine:

$$ h'_t = h_t + g_t\cdot E_\text{ngram} $$

where g is a learned gate.

Initially:

65536 entries
× 32 dimensions
× INT8
≈ 2 MB

Beautifully manageable.

14. There is a useful negative result to keep in mind

A recent independent experiment applying Engram-like tables to small 0.5B–4B models found substantial perplexity improvements but essentially no consistent gain on HellaSwag, PIQA or ARC-Challenge.

That makes your experiment more interesting, not less.

We can directly measure:

                         Perplexity    reasoning    memory      speed
Dense baseline
+ recurrence
+ MoE
+ Engram
+ recurrence + MoE
+ MoE + Engram
+ all three

Instead of assuming that Engram must help.

15. The experimental progression I would use

This is where I think your project can become much more valuable than simply "another tiny LLM."

Stage	Architecture	Question
0	dense tiny transformer	Baseline
1	recurrent shared layers	Does repeated compute replace parameters?
2	dense + Engram	Does external memory improve PPL/tasks?
3	top-1 MoE	Can experts specialize?
4	top-2 MoE	Is quality worth doubled active compute?
5	recurrent MoE	Does expert selection change during reasoning?
6	recurrent MoE + Engram	Do memory and compute sparsity complement each other?
7	quantized	What quality is lost at INT8/INT4?
8	constrained expert cache	What does cache size do?
9	CPU/NPU hybrid	Can FreeToken-style scheduling help?
10	256-MB target	Can the complete architecture survive embedded deployment?

Every stage produces a measurable result.

That is considerably better pedagogically than starting with the final architecture.

16. Distillation: "from scratch" still makes sense

I would interpret "distilled from scratch" as:

Initialize the tiny model randomly, but train it partly from targets produced by a capable teacher.

We're not pruning or compressing an existing network.

We create our own:

tokenizer
architecture
router
experts
Engram
recursive computation

from scratch.

Then a larger teacher generates:

input → teacher output

and, where practical:

teacher token probability distribution

Student objective:

$$ L = \alpha L_\text{token} +\beta L_\text{KD} +\gamma L_\text{router} +\delta L_\text{balance} $$

Potentially later:

$$ +\epsilon L_\text{recurrence} $$

where intermediate recursive states are rewarded for progressively improving the answer.

We don't need a frontier teacher. A modest local 1B–7B model can generate vastly better training labels than our ~20M student.

17. Start with a constrained domain

I would not initially train it to be a general chatbot.

That confounds too many things.

I'd use a mixture like:

natural language
simple code
arithmetic
sequence transformations
logic puzzles
small algorithms
structured text

with synthetic data heavily represented.

Why?

Because then we can actually see whether experts specialize.

Imagine a router eventually producing:

arithmetic → experts 3,17
Rust syntax → experts 8,26
English prose → experts 2,14
sequence reasoning → experts 21,31

That's an educational result you can inspect.

18. Metrics should go far beyond perplexity

For every run I'd record:

Neural	Systems
validation loss	tokens/sec
perplexity	bytes/token
task accuracy	RAM peak
teacher/student KL	accelerator RAM
active params/token	expert cache hit rate
router entropy	expert transfers/token
expert load balance	CPU vs NPU work
expert specialization	energy/token
accuracy vs recursion	latency/token
Engram contribution	Engram collisions
Engram gate magnitude	cache reuse distance

FreeToken demonstrates why this matters: systems characteristics can dominate performance even when the mathematical model remains identical.

19. Your 256-MB / 0.5-TOPS target is plausible — with qualifications

Inference: absolutely plausible for this tiny architecture.

Training the complete system on-device: much less attractive.

A 20M-parameter model may require only about:

INT8   ~20 MB
INT4   ~10 MB

for deployed weights.

But Adam-style training might require roughly:

weights
gradients
master weights
first moment
second moment
activations

and quickly exceed 256 MB.

So I'd separate:

training machine
    ↓
quantized packed checkpoint
    ↓
256-MB inference device

and then optionally support limited on-device learning:

router adaptation
Engram updates
small expert fine-tuning
last-layer training

That would itself be an interesting experiment.

20. 0.5 TOPS probably isn't the real limit

For this design the limiting resource may be:

memory bandwidth and dispatch latency, not TOPS.

Suppose a token touches only ~1–3M parameters through recurrent sparse execution.

Even at several recurrent steps that's nowhere near a 0.5-TOPS theoretical arithmetic ceiling.

But if each tiny expert causes:

flash read
DMA setup
NPU submission
synchronization

the accelerator may spend more time launching experts than multiplying matrices.

Therefore I would design the NPU architecture around expert bundles rather than arbitrary individual networks.

For example:

expert-bank-0 = experts 0..7
expert-bank-1 = experts 8..15
...

and make the router's scheduling granular enough to suit the actual NPU compiler.

21. A more radical option: experts as low-rank deltas

For the smallest machine, I'd also test:

            shared FFN
                +
       selected expert delta

rather than completely separate FFNs.

Each expert becomes:

$$ \Delta W_e = A_eB_e $$

with rank perhaps 4 or 8.

Then you can afford hundreds of experts.

Example:

d = 256
rank = 8

expert parameters
≈ 2 × 256 × 8
= 4096

So:

256 experts ≈ 1M parameters

per expert location.

That gives you genuinely large expert populations while remaining tiny.

This may actually be a better fit for the 0.5-TOPS NPU because the big shared matrix remains static and accelerator-friendly.

22. My preferred eventual architecture

I would call the conceptual design something like µMoE-RM for now:

                   token IDs
                      │
            ┌─────────▼────────┐
            │ token embedding  │
            └─────────┬────────┘
                      │
       recent tokens ─┼─────────────┐
                      │             │
                      │       ┌─────▼─────┐
                      │       │  Engram   │
                      │       │ 2/3/4gram │
                      │       └─────┬─────┘
                      │             │
                 ┌────▼─────────────▼──┐
                 │ recurrent core      │◄──────┐
                 │ attention/state     │       │
                 └────────┬────────────┘       │
                          │                    │
                    ┌─────▼─────┐              │
                    │  router   │              │
                    └─────┬─────┘              │
                          │ top-k               │
                    ┌─────▼─────┐              │
             RAM/   │ expert    │              │
             flash──┤ cache     │              │
                    └─────┬─────┘              │
                          │                    │
             ┌────────────┼────────────┐       │
             │            │            │       │
          expert       expert       expert     │
             │            │            │       │
             └────────────┼────────────┘       │
                          │                    │
                     combine                   │
                          │                    │
                     state update ─────────────┘
                          │
                      LM head

It has three independent kinds of sparsity:

$$ \boxed{ \text{parameter sharing} + \text{conditional compute} + \text{conditional memory} } $$

namely:

recurrence → temporal parameter reuse

MoE       → compute sparsity

Engram    → memory lookup sparsity

FreeToken then adds a fourth:

expert cache → residency sparsity

That is a remarkably elegant little research system.

23. It also fits your older hardware progression unusually well

I would actually develop it downward:

RTX 3090 / 5060
       │
       ▼
normal training + profiling
       │
       ▼
RTX 3060 / P40
       │
       ▼
CPU-only old Xeon
       │
       ▼
small SBC
       │
       ▼
LicheeRV/SG2002-class
256 MB + ~0.5 TOPS NPU

At every step, constrain the previous system artificially:

64 MB expert cache
32 MB
16 MB
8 MB
...

before moving to the real hardware.

Then an embedded failure isn't mysterious—you already know approximately where the knee in the curve should occur.

The experiment I would build first

I would resist starting with language generation.

Build a ~5–10M parameter recurrent MoE, perhaps 16 experts with top-2, and train it on synthetic transformations plus tiny text.

Give it a 64K × 32 ≈ 2-MB Engram.

Then build a visual/instrumented runtime showing:

current token
↓
Engram addresses + retrieved values
↓
recursive iteration 1
    router → experts 3,7
recursive iteration 2
    router → experts 3,12
recursive iteration 3
    router → experts 9,12
↓
prediction

alongside:

expert cache
┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
│ E3 │ E7 │E12 │ E9 │... │
└────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘

hits     7
misses   2
loads    1
CPU      1
NPU      8

Once that works, scale the number of experts upward while keeping active parameters nearly constant.

That gives you a very clean experimental question:

$$ \textbf{How much model capacity can we add without adding proportional compute?} $$

Then add the second question:

$$ \textbf{How much of that capacity actually needs to reside near the accelerator?} $$

And finally the Engram question:

$$ \textbf{How much memorization can be removed from neural computation altogether?} $$

Those three questions connect TRM/HRM → MoE → Engram → FreeToken → your 256-MB NPU target much more coherently than simply trying to shrink an existing LLM.

I think this is strong enough to justify its own experimental repo rather than being merely another sw-mlpl demonstration: the repo could progressively implement Dense → Recursive → MoE → Engram → Cached MoE → Hybrid CPU/NPU, with every stage retaining comparable benchmarks and trace visualizations.

what would we call this new repo?

Given the repo's purpose—a small, inspectable experimental model that combines recursive reasoning, sparse MoE, Engram memory, and FreeToken-inspired memory hierarchy—I'd avoid naming it after any one of those techniques. The interesting thing is the combination.

My strongest candidates:

Name	Why it works
tiny-moe-lab	Immediately understandable; emphasizes experimentation
micro-moe	Short, memorable, emphasizes extreme scaling-down
recursive-moe	Captures perhaps the most novel architectural combination
sparse-reasoner	Describes the goal rather than implementation
tiny-sparse-reasoner	More explicit about scale
micro-reasoner	Nice if MoE/Engram are implementation details
tiny-conditional-model	Captures conditional compute + memory
micro-moe-reasoner	Descriptive without being too long
tiny-moe-research	Serious/academic sounding, but generic
moe-microscope	Excellent if education/visualization is central
I particularly like moe-microscope

It fits what we're actually proposing better than tiny-moe-lab.

The project isn't merely trying to create the smallest useful MoE. It's intended to let someone look inside one:

token
  ↓
Engram lookup ─────────► inspect
  ↓
recurrent state ───────► inspect
  ↓
router ────────────────► inspect
  ↓
expert selection ──────► inspect
  ↓
expert cache ──────────► inspect
  ↓
CPU/NPU scheduling ────► inspect
  ↓
prediction

And experiments can progressively turn mechanisms on:

dense
  → recursive
  → MoE
  → recursive MoE
  → + Engram
  → + quantization
  → + expert caching
  → + heterogeneous execution
  → tiny hardware

That makes moe-microscope a good description of the project's educational purpose rather than just its architecture.

It also connects nicely with the "ML microscope" concept we've discussed for your visualization work without tying the repository to sw-MLPL itself.

Another direction: mi

67	2. Prefill and decode are deliberately treated differently
68	
69	This is one of FreeToken's more interesting decisions.
70	
71	During generation, MoE routing is sparse. But during a long prompt, thousands of input tokens collectively tend to touch most experts. FreeToken found that trying to fetch individual experts on demand during prefill therefore doesn't buy much.
72	
73	Instead it allocates two complete expert-layer buffers. While the GPU executes layer L, it streams the experts for layer L+1. The buffers swap roles.
74	
75	Conceptually:
76	
77	time ─────────────────────────────────────────────>
78	
79	GPU:     compute L0 | compute L1 | compute L2 | compute L3
80	PCIe:       load L1 |    load L2 |    load L3 | load L4
81	             ^ overlap ^
82	
83	buffer A:     L0          L2          L4
84	buffer B:          L1          L3
85	
86	On an RTX 5090 the paper reports streaming a 64.4-GB expert pool at roughly 52.7 GB/s during an 8192-token prefill; removing the second buffer reduced throughput materially as prompt size increased.
87	
88	Your tiny implementation should reproduce this experiment even if the buffers contain only tens or hundreds of KB.
89	
90	That makes the effect visible rather than merely theoretical.

129	4. FreeToken's cleverest mechanism: q*
130	
131	Suppose a layer needs four experts that aren't in VRAM.
132	
133	A simplistic system has two choices:
134	
135	A: transfer all four → GPU
136	B: execute all four → CPU
137	
138	FreeToken instead does both simultaneously.
139	
140	It measures:
141	
142	B_P: pinned host→GPU transfer bandwidth
143	B_H: host-memory expert processing bandwidth
144	
145	and approximately chooses
146	
147	$$ q^* = m {B_P \over B_H} $$
148	
149	where m is the number of missing experts.
150	
151	So:
152	
153	               4 missing experts
154	                      |
155	          ┌───────────┴──────────┐
156	          │                      │
157	    transfer/cache           CPU execute
158	       expert 41             expert 52
159	                             expert 59
160	                             expert 63
161	          │                      │
162	        GPU                    CPU
163	          └───────────┬──────────┘
164	                      │
165	                  sum output
166	
167	Both outputs are exact partial MoE outputs; this is not an approximation of the model.
168	
169	That distinction is important.
170	
171	The scheduler is approximating the best resource allocation, not the neural computation.
172	
173	FreeToken now provides ft bench bw specifically to measure these characteristics on the target machine rather than guessing them from specifications.
174	
175	For your system I'd generalize this to:
176	
177	$$ q^* = f(B_\text{flash},B_\text{RAM},B_\text{DMA}, B_\text{CPU},B_\text{NPU}) $$
178	
179	That might actually become a genuinely interesting embedded-systems research result.

181	5. FreeToken also removes the scheduler from the critical path
182	
183	There is a less glamorous but important implementation trick.
184	
185	FreeToken keeps routing/cache decisions compatible with CUDA graph execution. Routing-dependent work—deduplicating experts, determining hits/misses, choosing LRU victims and translating logical expert numbers into physical slots—runs inside fixed graph machinery rather than bouncing repeatedly through Python/host scheduling.
186	
187	Its CPU side likewise uses persistent native worker threads pinned to physical cores, SIMD kernels, and in-kernel dequantization.
188	
189	For a 0.5-TOPS NPU, this lesson may matter even more than on CUDA:
190	
191	Do not make tiny expert dispatches expensive.
192	
193	A 30-µs neural expert isn't useful if selecting and launching it costs 100 µs.
194	
195	That argues strongly for a restricted routing scheme that can be ahead-of-time compiled.

197	6. Quantization helps twice
198	
199	FreeToken currently supports combinations including BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and MXFP4 depending on model/backend.
200	
201	For an offloaded MoE model quantization gives two benefits:
202	
203	$$ \text{smaller weights} \Rightarrow \begin{cases} \text{more experts fit in cache}\\ \text{less data crosses PCIe} \end{cases} $$
204	
205	That second property is particularly important.
206	
207	For your embedded system, INT4 expert weights may therefore be more useful than INT4 dense weights.

209	The shared network can initially remain INT8 while experts become INT4.

403	13. Add the Engram as another sparse axis
404	
405	DeepSeek describes Engram as complementary to MoE:
406	
407	MoE = conditional computation
408	Engram = conditional memory
409	
410	Engram performs deterministic N-gram addressing and retrieves learned memory values in essentially O(1), avoiding the need for neural layers to repeatedly reconstruct common token patterns. DeepSeek also emphasizes that deterministic addressing makes very large tables naturally offloadable.

413	
414	For recent tokens:
415	
416	"for" "(" "i"

418	compute:
419	
420	h2 = hash("(" ,"i")       % table_size
421	h3 = hash("for","(","i")  % table_size
422	
423	lookup:
424	
425	E2[h2]
426	E3[h3]
427	
428	then:
429	
430	engram = projection(E2 + E3)

432	and combine:
433	
434	$$ h'_t = h_t + g_t\cdot E_\text{ngram} $$
435	
436	where g is a learned gate.

438	Initially:
439	
440	65536 entries
441	× 32 dimensions
442	× INT8
443	≈ 2 MB
